messages.author: 6adfdf8a41ea977e
messages.subject: userGWAS for second order factor?
parts:
Hi,

I ran into a couple questions when using Genomis SEM.

1) Is it possible to obtain summary statistics for a second order latent factor? Usermodel function seems to produce a decent model fit (see below), however, when the same model is specified via userGWAS function, all the rows return negative residual variances (even when residual variances are constrained to be positive). 

Am I going the wrong way about it or is it simply not possible to obtain summary statistics for a second order latent variable? 

Model
model <- "F1 =~ HDL + TG + LDL + WC 
F2 =~ HbA1c + SBP + WC 
L1 =~ F1 + F2 + DEP 
HbA1c ~~ a*HbA1c 
a > .001" 

Model fit indices
chisq: 20.00313  
df: 11    
p_chisq: 0.045 
AIC: 54.003      
CFI: 0.9235 
SRMR: 0.0775

2) In a separate analysis, I ran a multivariate GWAS of three traits and obtained 6 independent genome-wide significant SNPs. However, when I located the genome-wide significant SNPs in the original univariate GWASs of the three traits, I found that only one SNP was significant at a genome-wide level for one of the traits, and the rest were p > .03. Is this to be expected or does it mean there is some sort of error in my analysis? 

Any advice is much appreciated. 

Kind regards,

Vilte

messages.author: d6d83e22ef3ba9f1
messages.subject: Re: userGWAS for second order factor?
parts:
Hi Vilte, 

Glad you are using the package! Responses below: 

1. It is possible to estimate SNP effects for a higher order factor. Can you share the full code you ran for the usermodel and higher order factor GWAS? 

2. What are the univariate GWAS betas across the traits for those hits that are highly significant for one trait but not the others? I would expect this behavior in a couple of instances. The first would be if all of the indicators have similarly sized loadings on the factor, and the univariate GWAS betas are also similarly sized, in which case the univariate SNP effects conform to the factor structure, would not be down-weighted for the estimated SNP effects, and would be estimated as a hit. Another scenario where this might occur is if you have one indicator that has a much larger loading on the factor, and this is also the better powered indicator, or at least the indicator for which the SNP was also a hit in the univariate GWAS. In this case, the model is both prioritizing that indicator more and, therefore, it will be pulled in as a hit. The third scenario would be that you the univariate GWAS betas are highly dissimilar, in which case the model might still estimate it as a factor hit, but I would also expect the Q_SNP metric--designed to capture SNPs that strongly deviate from the factor structure--to be significant, or at least fairly large. Q_SNP is automatically calculated in the context of the commonfactorGWAS function and can be calculated using a two-step procedure using the userGWAS function that we outline on the github. 

Best, 
  Andrew

parts:
Hi Andrew,

I realised I replied to your personal email account, so I am copy-pasting my response here as well: 

1. I have attached an .Rmd and .html documents containing the full code for the higher order factor GWAS. The html file does not portray the error message but essentially after running userGWAS each row of the output contained NAs and "lavaan WARNING: some estimated lv variances are negative". 

2. The standardised loadings for each of the three traits were: CAD: 0.77, T2D: 0.51, DEP: 0.25. While CAD had a larger loading on the common factor, its sample size was substantially smaller than the other two traits and all univariate p-values also > .025. I wonder if it could be due to the third scenario you specified. I thought because the Q_chisq_pval is not significant at the genome-wide level, the evidence for heterogeneity was not very strong. Or would you interpret the Q statistic differently? I have included two .csv files, one containing the 6 independent SNPs with the Q statistic and another one with the univariate betas. 

P.S. I don't know whether it is of any relevance but when looking at the Q_chisq for the total number of genome-wide significant hits (before clumping was performed) many SNPs had smaller Q statistics, ranging from 3.14 to 21.66 (with 10 being the median).

(The attachments are included in my original email, let me know whether you would like me to post them here as well.)

Best wishes,
Vilte

messages.author: d6d83e22ef3ba9f1
messages.subject: Re: userGWAS for second order factor?
parts:
Hi Vilte, 

Thanks for following up on this and for sending along your code. For your first question regarding estimating the SNP effects on the second-order latent factor I think your model was initially running into issues because you were simultaneously estimating the SNP effect on the second-order and first-order factors, which is resulting in negative variance estimates for your latent variables and likely increasing your run time quite a bit. I see that you also ran a model in which you only estimated the SNP effect on the higher=order factor, and then separately tried to run a model in which you estimate SNP effects on both the first and second-order factors and constrain the residuals to be above 0. I would try combining these two approaches: only estimate SNP effects on the second-order factor and then additionally constrain the residual variances of both the observed variables and the first-order latent variables. Note also regarding run time that running in parallel (the default for the GWAS functions) tends to only speed things up when running a larger set of SNPs because it can take a minute to initialize and stitch results back together on the back-end once done running in parallel. So just a side note that you might try setting parallel to FALSE just for these test runs of 100 SNPs, or try running closer to 5K SNPs to get a better sense of your run time for the larger set of SNPs. 

For your second question, based on the summary statistics you passed along I think you have scenarios 1 and 3 going on . For rs599839 and rs9369640 the univariate betas are directionally discordant across the three indicators and Q is more significant here (2.93E-5 and 6.05E-5), which lines up with the third scenario I described. For the remaining SNPs it seems that you have SNPs that conform to the factor model in their patterning of univariate betas, with the largest value for CAD2, smaller for T2D2, and smallest for DEP, which mirrors the ordering of factor loadings. So you might consider writing these results up by noting that those first two SNPs should be interpreted with caution and re-evaluated at larger sample sizes, while the remaining four are more likely to operate via the common factor. 


Best, 

  Andrew

messages.subject: Re: userGWAS for second order factor?
parts:
Hi Andrew,

Thank you very much for your response. 

Based on your response I specified the following model for the second-order factor:

model <- "F1 =~ HDL + TG + LDL + WC  
F2 =~ HbA1c + SBP + WC

L1 =~ F1 + F2 + DEP_full
HDL ~~ a*HDL
TG ~~ b*TG
LDL ~~ c*LDL
WC ~~ d*WC
HbA1c ~~ f*HbA1c
SBP ~~ e*SBP
DEP_full ~~ g*DEP_full
F1 ~~ h*F1
F2 ~~ i*F2
a > .001
b > .001
c > .001
d > .001
e > .001
f > .001
g > .001
h > .001
i > .001
L1 ~ SNP"

Is this what you had in mind? Because when I run it, I still obtain the same output with NAs and negative residual variance within every single row. Are you aware of anything else that could be causing the error? 

With regard to my second question, due to the presence of heterogeneity for some of the lead SNPs, I attempted to impose equality constraints on the factor loadings of all three traits. When I did that, I noticed that the CFI changed depending on whether I chose to use unit variance identification for the latent factor or constrained the loading of the first factor to be equal to 1. I thought that model fit indices should remain the same, regardless of whether we choose to set the std.lv parameter to TRUE or FALSE. Is the discrepancy in CFI values to be expected when imposing equality constraints? If so, which of the models (latent factor variance = 1 vs. factor loading = 1) is more appropriate for running a userGWAS? I have attached an .html file demonstrating the change in CFI values.

I appreciate your help and apologise for the number of questions. 

Best wishes,

Vilte

messages.author: d6d83e22ef3ba9f1
messages.subject: Re: userGWAS for second order factor?
parts:
Hi Vilte, 

That is the model I had in mind; it could be that when you go from using unit variance ID in the model without SNPs to unit variance ID that this causes some issues. You might try telling lavaan to freely estimate the first factor loading by writing NA* for the first indicator and then fix the residual variance of the factors to 1 and see if that helps. If not, feel free to send me the ldsc output and first 100 rows of the sumstats output and I can take a closer look. 

For your second question, you are correct to expect unit loading and unit variance ID to produce equivalent model fit as you observe for model chi-square, AIC, and SRMR.  For CFI estimates, there was a specific bug when using unit variance ID with equality constraints on the factor loadings that was causing the CFI estimates to be underestimated. I’ve put in a fix for that if you want to redownload the package and restart R; you should find then that you get the CFI estimate you were previously getting for your second model for both the unit loading and unit variance ID. Thanks very much for catching that! With that said, in my opinion imposing equality constraints on the loadings is not necessarily the way to go because it is going to cause misfit to your data. Rather, I would say that given the data you seem to have some SNPs that plausibly operate via the factor structure and some that do not. This is generally to be expected, and not something I would try and solve per se, but of course that is just my opinion and that decision point is up to you. 


Best, 

  Andrew

Hi Vilte, 

Glad you are using the package! Responses below: 

1. It is possible to estimate SNP effects for a higher order factor. Can you share the full code you ran for the usermodel and higher order factor GWAS? 

2. What are the univariate GWAS betas across the traits for those hits that are highly significant for one trait but not the others? I would expect this behavior in a couple of instances. The first would be if all of the indicators have similarly sized loadings on the factor, and the univariate GWAS betas are also similarly sized, in which case the univariate SNP effects conform to the factor structure, would not be down-weighted for the estimated SNP effects, and would be estimated as a hit. Another scenario where this might occur is if you have one indicator that has a much larger loading on the factor, and this is also the better powered indicator, or at least the indicator for which the SNP was also a hit in the univariate GWAS. In this case, the model is both prioritizing that indicator more and, therefore, it will be pulled in as a hit. The third scenario would be that you the univariate GWAS betas are highly dissimilar, in which case the model might still estimate it as a factor hit, but I would also expect the Q_SNP metric--designed to capture SNPs that strongly deviate from the factor structure--to be significant, or at least fairly large. Q_SNP is automatically calculated in the context of the commonfactorGWAS function and can be calculated using a two-step procedure using the userGWAS function that we outline on the github. 

Best, 
  Andrew

Hi Vilte, 

That is the model I had in mind; it could be that when you go from using unit variance ID in the model without SNPs to unit variance ID that this causes some issues. You might try telling lavaan to freely estimate the first factor loading by writing NA* for the first indicator and then fix the residual variance of the factors to 1 and see if that helps. If not, feel free to send me the ldsc output and first 100 rows of the sumstats output and I can take a closer look. 

For your second question, you are correct to expect unit loading and unit variance ID to produce equivalent model fit as you observe for model chi-square, AIC, and SRMR.  For CFI estimates, there was a specific bug when using unit variance ID with equality constraints on the factor loadings that was causing the CFI estimates to be underestimated. I’ve put in a fix for that if you want to redownload the package and restart R; you should find then that you get the CFI estimate you were previously getting for your second model for both the unit loading and unit variance ID. Thanks very much for catching that! With that said, in my opinion imposing equality constraints on the loadings is not necessarily the way to go because it is going to cause misfit to your data. Rather, I would say that given the data you seem to have some SNPs that plausibly operate via the factor structure and some that do not. This is generally to be expected, and not something I would try and solve per se, but of course that is just my opinion and that decision point is up to you. 


Best, 

  Andrew

On Tue, 2 Mar 2021 at 01:44, agro...@gmail.com <agro...@gmail.com> wrote:

Hi Vilte, 

Thanks for following up on this and for sending along your code. For your first question regarding estimating the SNP effects on the second-order latent factor I think your model was initially running into issues because you were simultaneously estimating the SNP effect on the second-order and first-order factors, which is resulting in negative variance estimates for your latent variables and likely increasing your run time quite a bit. I see that you also ran a model in which you only estimated the SNP effect on the higher=order factor, and then separately tried to run a model in which you estimate SNP effects on both the first and second-order factors and constrain the residuals to be above 0. I would try combining these two approaches: only estimate SNP effects on the second-order factor and then additionally constrain the residual variances of both the observed variables and the first-order latent variables. Note also regarding run time that running in parallel (the default for the GWAS functions) tends to only speed things up when running a larger set of SNPs because it can take a minute to initialize and stitch results back together on the back-end once done running in parallel. So just a side note that you might try setting parallel to FALSE just for these test runs of 100 SNPs, or try running closer to 5K SNPs to get a better sense of your run time for the larger set of SNPs. 

For your second question, based on the summary statistics you passed along I think you have scenarios 1 and 3 going on . For rs599839 and rs9369640 the univariate betas are directionally discordant across the three indicators and Q is more significant here (2.93E-5 and 6.05E-5), which lines up with the third scenario I described. For the remaining SNPs it seems that you have SNPs that conform to the factor model in their patterning of univariate betas, with the largest value for CAD2, smaller for T2D2, and smallest for DEP, which mirrors the ordering of factor loadings. So you might consider writing these results up by noting that those first two SNPs should be interpreted with caution and re-evaluated at larger sample sizes, while the remaining four are more likely to operate via the common factor. 


Best, 

  Andrew
